title: Checking if a Binary Tree is Height-Balanced

phrases.explanation: A tree where the left and right subtree heights of every node differ by at most one

concept: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether the tree is height-balanced. A binary tree is balanced if for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by no more than one.

solutions.label: Top-Down Recursion
solutions.summary: For each node, compute the height of its left and right subtrees separately using a helper function, then check the balance condition. This recalculates heights repeatedly.

solutions.label: Bottom-Up Recursion with Early Termination
solutions.summary: Compute height and check balance in a single pass using post-order traversal. Return negative one immediately if any subtree is unbalanced.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's today's problem. You're given the root of a binary tree. I'd like you to determine whether the tree is height-balanced. A tree is balanced when the depth of the left and right subtrees of every single node never differs by more than one.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So I need to check every node, not just the root. A few questions: can the tree be empty, meaning the root is null? And what should I return in that case?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the root can be null. An empty tree is considered balanced, so return true. The function signature takes a TreeNode root and returns a boolean.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. And just to confirm, a single node with no children is also balanced, right? What about the size of the tree?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Correct, a single node is balanced. The tree can have up to five thousand nodes, and node values range from negative ten thousand to ten thousand, but the values don't matter for this problem.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Alright, so the task is: for every node in the tree, check that the height difference between its left and right subtrees is at most one. If all nodes satisfy this, return true; otherwise return false. Let me think about approaches.

sections.diagram:

    C --> D((15))
    C --> E((7))
    F["Check node 3: left height=0, right height=1, diff=1 ✓"]
    G["Check node 20: left height=0, right height=0, diff=0 ✓"]
    H["Result: Balanced ✓"]
    F --> G --> H
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style D fill:#93c5fd,color:#000
    style E fill:#93c5fd,color:#000
    style H fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Off the top of my head, I can write a helper function that calculates the height of any node. Then for each node, I call this helper on its left child and right child, check if the difference is more than one, and recurse into both subtrees.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That makes sense. Can you walk through the example tree? Root is three, left child is nine, right child is twenty, and twenty has children fifteen and seven.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. At node three, left subtree height is zero since nine is a leaf, and right subtree height is one since twenty has children. The difference is one, so node three is fine. Then I check node twenty: both children are leaves, heights are zero, difference is zero. Nodes nine, fifteen, and seven are leaves, so they're trivially balanced. The tree is balanced.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good. What's the time complexity here?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For each of the n nodes, I compute height which takes O of n in the worst case. So the total time is O of n-squared. Space is O of n for the recursion stack in a skewed tree. This works but the repeated height calculations are wasteful.

sections.title: Bottom-Up Recursion with Early Termination
sections.diagram:
graph BT
    D((15)) -->|height 0| C((20))
    E((7)) -->|height 0| C
    B((9)) -->|height 0| A((3))
    C -->|height 1| A
    F["Post-order: visit 9→0, 15→0, 7→0, 20→1, 3→1"]
    G["All diffs ≤ 1 → Balanced ✓"]
    F --> G
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style D fill:#c4b5fd,color:#000
    style E fill:#c4b5fd,color:#000
    style G fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can do better with a bottom-up approach. Instead of computing height separately, I write one recursive function that returns the height of a subtree but also checks balance along the way. If a subtree is unbalanced, I return negative one to signal failure.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Let me walk through this with the same tree. How does the post-order traversal work here?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We visit leaves first. Node nine returns height zero. Fifteen and seven each return zero. Node twenty gets left height zero, right height zero, difference is zero, so it returns max of zero and zero plus one, which is one. Node three gets left zero, right one, difference one, returns max of zero and one plus one, which is two. No negative one was returned, so the tree is balanced.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And if the tree were unbalanced?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: As soon as any node finds a height difference greater than one, or receives negative one from a child, it immediately returns negative one. This short-circuits and bubbles up to the root. Time complexity is O of n since we visit each node exactly once. Space is O of n for the call stack.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice work. Can you summarize both approaches?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The top-down approach checks each node by computing subtree heights separately, giving O of n-squared time. The bottom-up approach combines height calculation and balance checking into one traversal, achieving O of n time. Both use O of n space for recursion. The key insight is that by returning height and balance information together, we avoid redundant computation.
